script.opening: "Hi doctor. My right nostril keeps blocking up and there's been a bit of blood in the discharge, on and off for weeks. I get hay fever, so I figured it's that, or a sinus infection. Could you sort me a steroid spray or some antihistamines? My left side's completely fine, it's just the right. I'm sure it's nothing — just need to clear it up."

facts.text: About two months. Right side blocked all the time, not just in summer. Blood-streaked mucus most mornings. Three nosebleeds from the right side in the last month, stopped on their own. Left side clear. No sneezing or itchy eyes now.
Hay fever every June and July — both sides, sneezing, itchy eyes, settles with antihistamines. This is "different — it's autumn and it's only one side".
Right ear feels blocked and dull for about a month, "like being on a plane". No pain, no discharge.

facts.topic: Neck — only if asked about lumps
facts.text: A painless lump on the right side of your neck below the ear, noticed about three weeks ago, "about the size of a grape".
No double vision, no facial numbness, no headaches, no swelling of the cheek, no loose teeth. Weight steady. No foreign body.
Hay fever (cetirizine in summer). No other medicines, no allergies, not on blood thinners. Non-smoker. No woodwork or leather work.
Born in Hong Kong, family originally from Guangdong; moved to the UK at 20. An uncle in Hong Kong had "nose cancer".
52, restaurant owner, married, two teenagers. Drinks little.

Polite, practical, wanting a spray. Answer the ear and neck questions honestly when asked. If the doctor explains that one-sided blockage with blood needs a specialist camera check soon, you become worried: "My uncle had cancer in the nose. Is it that?" Accept urgent referral and an in-person check if explained calmly.

ice.ideas: "It's hay fever or a sinus infection."
ice.concerns: Mostly the nuisance. Underneath (only if asked): your uncle's nose cancer.
ice.expectations: "A steroid spray or antihistamines." You will accept referral if the reasons are explained.

cues: "It's just the right side." — say in the opening.
"My right ear feels blocked too." — say if asked about other symptoms.
"My uncle had something in his nose." — say if asked about family history.

checkpoints.text: Applies the ONE-SIDED RULE: recognises UNILATERAL persistent nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge / recurrent unilateral epistaxis as a RED FLAG (possible sinonasal or nasopharyngeal tumour) — distinct from benign BILATERAL allergic rhinitis — and does NOT treat it as "hay fever" with a spray/antihistamine

Elicits the NASOPHARYNGEAL/head-and-neck red flags by directed history: a NECK LUMP, UNILATERAL serous otitis media/blocked ear, blood-stained nasal discharge, and any cranial-nerve symptoms — and the ETHNICITY-related risk (Southern Chinese/Southeast Asian)

Arranges a prompt face-to-face examination of the nose (anterior rhinoscopy), ears (otoscopy) and neck/lymph nodes — none of which can be done on video — without delaying the referral, recognising a unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult and an unexplained neck lump as themselves warranting urgent referral

Refers URGENTLY to ENT for nasendoscopy/assessment to exclude tumour (sinonasal/nasopharyngeal carcinoma), rather than trialling allergy treatment for a unilateral problem; recognises the suspected cancer pathway criteria that apply: NICE NG12 — an unexplained neck lump at 45+ (laryngeal) or a persistent unexplained neck lump (oral); NICE NG98 — hearing loss with a middle-ear effusion not associated with an upper respiratory tract infection in an adult of Chinese or south-east Asian family origin. NG12 has no nasal criterion
Keeps the benign differential in mind (polyp, foreign body, deviated septum) but does NOT let it justify allergy treatment without examination/referral for persistent unilateral symptoms
Does not accept the "hay fever" framing for unilateral symptoms; surfaces the noticed neck lump and the underlying fear, naming the concern proportionately
Reassures proportionately (many causes are benign; we examine and refer to be sure) so he accepts assessment, and addresses the reluctance to make a fuss/take time off

Safety-nets and follows up: the urgent ENT referral and what to expect (nasendoscopy), what to report (worsening, the lump enlarging, new neurological/visual symptoms), and a follow-up — investigating the one-sided red flag, not treating allergy

worked.txt: "I can see why you’d think hay fever — but there’s an important difference that changes my plan: hay fever affects BOTH sides, with sneezing and clear runny nose. Yours is just the ONE nostril, persistently blocked, with blood in it. Persistent one-sided nose symptoms like that we always check properly, because occasionally there’s something on that side we need to find. So a spray isn’t the right answer here."

"A few questions: has your hearing or your ear on that same right side felt blocked? … And have you noticed any lump in your neck? … You have. And can I ask about family background — anyone of Southern Chinese heritage? … Those things together are exactly why I want this looked at, not treated as allergy."

"Let me be straight: persistent one-sided blockage with bleeding, a blocked ear on the same side, and a neck lump, I need to refer urgently to make sure there’s nothing growing at the back of the nose. It might well be something harmless like a polyp — but the only safe way to know is for a specialist to look. And if it were something more, catching it early really matters."

"So I’m referring you urgently to the ear-nose-throat specialists — they’ll pass a tiny camera through the nose to look at the back of it and check your neck. That’s the right step, and it’s why antihistamines wouldn’t have sorted it."

"I know you didn’t want to make a fuss or take time off — but you’ve done exactly the right thing, and this is worth a couple of hours. The lump you’d noticed is a real reason to get checked, not to worry alone about."

"If the bleeding gets heavier, the lump grows, or you get double vision, numbness in the face or worsening hearing, tell us sooner. I’ll get the urgent referral done and follow it up. You came for a hay-fever spray; what you actually needed was to have this one-sided problem looked at properly."

f.learning: The one-sided rule: UNILATERAL persistent nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge or recurrent unilateral epistaxis is a RED FLAG (possible sinonasal or nasopharyngeal tumour) and must NOT be treated as "hay fever" — benign allergic rhinitis is typically BILATERAL, seasonal, with sneezing/itch and clear discharge. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma classically presents with a NECK LUMP (often first), UNILATERAL serous otitis media/blocked ear (Eustachian obstruction), blood-stained nasal discharge and cranial-nerve signs, with higher risk in people of Southern Chinese/Southeast Asian origin — so elicit these red flags and the ethnicity-related risk, examine the nose/ears/neck (a unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult and an unexplained neck lump each warrant urgent referral), and refer urgently to ENT for nasendoscopy rather than trialling allergy treatment for a one-sided problem. Keep the benign differential (polyp, foreign body, deviated septum) in mind but do not let it justify allergy treatment without examination/referral. The hidden agenda is the "hay fever" misconception plus avoidance masking a noticed neck lump and quiet fear; don’t accept the framing, surface the fear, reassure proportionately, and refer. Unilateral persistent nasal obstruction/epistaxis can also be benign (e.g. a polyp, foreign body, deviated septum), but the one-sided pattern mandates examination and ENT referral to exclude tumour — you cannot reassure it away as allergy. NPC caught earlier has better outcomes.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG98 (hearing loss in adults, 2018) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
knowledge.summary: Persistent one-sided nasal blockage with blood-stained discharge is not hay fever. With a same-side blocked ear, a neck lump and Southern Chinese family origin, nasopharyngeal carcinoma must be excluded by urgent ENT assessment with nasendoscopy.

points.t: Allergic rhinitis is typically bilateral, with sneezing, itch and clear discharge. Persistent unilateral obstruction, blood-stained discharge or recurrent same-side epistaxis needs examination and ENT assessment: causes range from polyp or septal deviation to sinonasal or nasopharyngeal tumour.

A neck lump (often the first sign), a unilateral middle-ear effusion or blocked ear from Eustachian tube obstruction, nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge, and cranial nerve symptoms such as double vision or facial numbness. Incidence is higher in people of Southern Chinese and south-east Asian family origin; EBV-associated.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with an unexplained lump in the neck, and for oral cancer with a persistent unexplained neck lump. At 52 with an unexplained neck lump he meets this; the head and neck team assesses the nasopharynx too.

NICE NG98 (2018): consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT for adults of Chinese or south-east Asian family origin who have hearing loss and a middle-ear effusion not associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. Confirm the effusion on otoscopy at a face-to-face review.
Video cannot replace anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy and neck palpation. Arrange a prompt face-to-face examination, but the history alone justifies the urgent referral; do not wait for a spray trial.
Heavy epistaxis that will not stop with pressure, or new cranial nerve signs (double vision, facial numbness, drooping), stridor or difficulty swallowing need same-day assessment.

dg.d: Open question; lets him describe the one-sided pattern; parks the spray request without dismissing it.
Work pressure and reluctance to take time off; what he has read online; who is at home to support him.
Face-to-face anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy for effusion and neck examination; nasendoscopy via ENT; no spray trial first.
Nasopharyngeal or sinonasal carcinoma versus polyp, septal deviation, foreign body or infection; allergic rhinitis argued against by the one-sided pattern.
Asks about cranial nerve symptoms, swallowing, weight loss and ethnicity-related risk; recognises the neck lump and unilateral ear as red flags.
States that a tumour must be excluded and explains why this is not hay fever, while acknowledging benign causes.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral today (NICE NG12 neck lump criterion; NICE NG98 ear criterion if effusion confirmed); face-to-face examination this week.
Addresses the work barrier practically (early slot, work letter); no allergy treatment as a substitute for referral.
A&E for uncontrolled epistaxis; same-day contact for cranial nerve symptoms, stridor, dysphagia or a fast-growing lump; ring if no appointment within a week.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up the withheld neck lump, the “different from my usual hay fever” comment and the same-side blocked ear.
Idea (hay fever or sinus); concern (quiet worry about cancer after reading online); expectation (spray, but also wants certainty).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Mostly the nuisance. Underneath (only if asked): your uncle's nose cancer — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Chen, I’m Dr Patel. I’ve read your form about the right side of your nose. Before I ask anything specific, tell me in your own words how it’s been.
model.why: Open start that lets him set out the story

model.text: It’s just the right nostril. Blocked for weeks, bit of blood in the discharge, the odd nosebleed. I get hay fever, so I figured it’s that or a sinus thing. If you could sort a steroid spray or antihistamines, that’d be great.
Thank you, that’s a clear account. I’d like to understand it properly first, then talk about what will help, and I promise we’ll come back to the spray. Is that alright?
model.why: Agrees an agenda and parks the request without dismissing it

model.text: Sure, go ahead.
When your hay fever usually flares, what does it feel like? Is it both sides, with sneezing and itching?
model.why: Contrasts his usual bilateral allergy with the current one-sided picture

model.text: Yes, normally both sides, sneezing, itchy eyes. This is different, I suppose. No sneezing, just the right side stuffed up, and the blood.
That difference matters, so thank you. Has your hearing or the ear on that same right side felt blocked or dull at all?
model.why: Asks for the same-side ear symptom that points to the nasopharynx

model.text: Now you mention it, yes. The right ear’s felt full, like on a plane. Muffled.
And have you noticed any lumps or swellings in your neck?
model.why: Directly asks about the commonest presenting sign

model.text: (pauses) There’s a small lump on the right side, under the jaw. I found it a few weeks ago. I didn’t put it on the form.
I’m really glad you’ve told me. Any double vision, numbness in your face, headaches, trouble swallowing, or weight loss?
model.why: Screens for cranial nerve involvement and systemic features

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Can I ask about your family background? Some nose and throat conditions are more common in particular communities, so it helps me.
model.why: Establishes the ethnicity-related risk sensitively and explains why

model.text: My family’s from southern China.
You mentioned the lump almost quietly, and you left it off the form. I wonder whether it’s been on your mind more than you’ve let on?
model.why: Names the cue of the withheld lump gently

model.text: Honestly, yes. I’ve read a bit online, and I know some of this is more common in people like me. I kept telling myself it’s hay fever because I didn’t want to make a fuss or take time off work.
That makes complete sense, and you haven’t made a fuss at all. What were you hoping we’d do today, really?
model.why: Validates the worry and elicits his real expectation

model.text: Part of me wanted you to say spray, done. The other part wants to know it’s nothing.

I’ll be straight with you. Hay fever affects both sides. A nose that’s blocked and bleeding on one side for weeks, with the ear blocked on the same side and a new lump in the neck, is a combination we always check with a specialist, quickly. A spray wouldn’t be the right answer.
model.why: Applies the one-sided rule and declines allergy treatment with a reason

model.text: Check for what, exactly?

The honest answer is that we need to be sure there’s nothing growing at the back of the nose, including a cancer. Many of these turn out to be something harmless, like a polyp. But with your symptoms and your background, the safe thing is an urgent look, and if it were something serious, finding it early really helps.
model.why: Names the possibility of cancer honestly and proportionately

model.text: (quiet) Okay. I think I knew that’s what you’d say.
That’s a lot to hear on a video call. How are you doing with it?
model.why: Pauses to check his emotional response before moving on

model.text: I’m alright. Better knowing than wondering.

Here’s the plan. I’m sending an urgent referral today to the head and neck specialists, which means an appointment within two weeks. They’ll pass a thin camera into the nose to look at the back of it and examine your neck, and they may arrange a scan or a sample.
model.why: Makes the suspected cancer pathway referral and explains nasendoscopy

model.text: I’d also like to see you in person this week, so I can look in your nose and ears and feel that lump properly. That won’t hold up the referral.
model.why: Arranges the examination video cannot provide without delaying referral

model.text: Work’s the tricky bit. Two appointments…
I understand. This is worth the time, and I can give you a letter for work if it helps. Could you manage early morning for my appointment?
model.why: Addresses the practical barrier rather than overriding it

model.text: Early is fine. Thanks.

If you have a nosebleed that won’t stop after 15 minutes of pinching, go to A&E. Contact us the same day if you get double vision, numbness in your face, trouble swallowing or breathing, or if the lump grows quickly. And if you haven’t heard about the hospital appointment within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.
model.why: Specific safety-net plus a hand-off check on the referral

model.text: Okay. Got it.
So that I know I’ve explained it well, how would you describe today’s plan to someone at home?
Not hay fever. Urgent camera check within two weeks, you’ll see me this week, and I ring if the bleeding’s bad or anything new happens.
Exactly right. You did the right thing coming in. I’ll see you this week.
model.why: Closes with a clear summary and follow-up

social.t: Reluctance to take time off is a common reason for delayed presentation. Offer early slots and a letter confirming hospital appointments; urgent appointments should not be traded for work pressure.
Patients who have read about a condition linked to their background may present with a “safe” explanation. Invite the worry explicitly and correct misinformation.

legal.t: Cancer is a disability under the Equality Act from diagnosis. If a diagnosis follows, he is protected from less favourable treatment at work and entitled to reasonable adjustments, including time off for treatment.

professional.t: Family origin changes the prior probability of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is written into NICE NG98. Ask with an explanation and record it; this is good clinical care, not stereotyping.
GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise the limits of a remote consultation. Arrange examination in person, but do not let it delay an urgent referral the history already justifies.
Suspected cancer pathway referrals should be tracked by the practice; tell the patient what to expect and when to chase.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support and the Mouth Cancer Foundation (head and neck) offer information in plain language, including while waiting for tests.

redFlags: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge or recurrent same-side epistaxis
Unexplained neck lump; unilateral blocked ear or middle-ear effusion in an adult
Cranial nerve symptoms (double vision, facial numbness), dysphagia, weight loss; Southern Chinese or south-east Asian family origin
psychosocial: Reluctance to take time off work and to “make a fuss”
What he has read online and how it has affected him
Who is around to support him through urgent tests

Concern: quiet fear about the neck lump and blocked ear after reading online
Expectation: a spray or antihistamine, while wanting to know it’s nothing

playbook.diagnosis: “This isn’t behaving like hay fever. One-sided blockage and bleeding for weeks, with the ear blocked on the same side and a lump in the neck, means we need to rule out something growing at the back of the nose, including cancer. Many causes turn out to be harmless, but this needs an urgent specialist look.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Hay fever is like a whole road flooding: both lanes, both sides. When only one lane is blocked, and it keeps bleeding, we look for something sitting in that lane. The specialists have a thin camera that can see right to the back.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been carrying the worry about that lump on your own, and hoping it was hay fever. Let’s get it checked properly and quickly, so you’re not left wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the work pressure and offer an early face-to-face slot and a work letter, so the urgent referral actually happens.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to head and neck ENT today (NICE NG12 neck lump criterion; NICE NG98 if an effusion is confirmed)
Face-to-face examination this week: anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy, neck
No steroid spray or antihistamine as a substitute for assessment
safetyNet: A&E for a nosebleed that won’t stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Same-day contact for double vision, facial numbness, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or a rapidly growing lump; ring if no appointment within a week

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can hold a red-flag rule against a plausible benign story. Candidates fail it by accepting “hay fever”, by missing the questions that reveal the lump and the ear, or by referring without explaining why.

items.fail: Prescribing a steroid nasal spray or antihistamine and asking him to come back if it doesn’t settle.
items.why: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with bleeding needs assessment, not an allergy trial. This is “management not in line with current UK practice” and delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
items.fix: State the one-sided rule and refer: “Hay fever affects both sides; this needs a specialist look.”

items.fail: Never asking about the ear on the same side or about a neck lump.
items.why: He does not volunteer the lump. Without directed questions, the data gathering misses the two features that make the referral urgent.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any blocked ear on that side? Any lumps in your neck?”

items.fail: Avoiding the question of family origin because it feels awkward.
items.why: Southern Chinese family origin substantially raises the risk of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and appears in NICE NG98. Leaving it out weakens the reasoning.
items.fix: Ask with a reason: “Some conditions are more common in particular communities; can I ask about your background?”

items.fail: Moving straight past the lump he mentions hesitantly and never asking how he feels about it.
items.why: The withheld lump is the cue to his hidden worry. Missing it reads as “does not respond to cues”.
items.fix: “You left the lump off the form. Has it been worrying you more than you’ve said?”

items.fail: Delaying the referral until he can be examined face to face.
items.why: Examination matters, but the history alone justifies urgent referral; waiting risks weeks of delay.
items.fix: Refer today and examine this week in parallel.

items.fail: Saying “it’s probably nothing” or, at the other extreme, “this could be cancer” with no context.
items.why: False reassurance undermines urgency; bare alarm frightens and disengages. Both lose Relating marks.
items.fix: Honest and proportionate: “We need to rule out a cancer; many causes are harmless; finding anything early matters.”

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll be in touch” and no specific safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the triggers (uncontrolled bleeding, double vision, facial numbness, swallowing or breathing problems) and when to chase the appointment.

The honest answer is that we need to be sure there’s nothing growing at the back of the nose, including a cancer. Many of these turn out to be something harmless, like a polyp. But with your symptoms and your background, the safe thing is an urgent look, and if it were something serious, finding it early really helps.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the possibility of cancer honestly and proportionately

SCA_MODELS.text: (quiet) Okay. I think I knew that’s what you’d say.
That’s a lot to hear on a video call. How are you doing with it?
SCA_MODELS.why: Pauses to check his emotional response before moving on

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m alright. Better knowing than wondering.

Here’s the plan. I’m sending an urgent referral today to the head and neck specialists, which means an appointment within two weeks. They’ll pass a thin camera into the nose to look at the back of it and examine your neck, and they may arrange a scan or a sample.
SCA_MODELS.why: Makes the suspected cancer pathway referral and explains nasendoscopy

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d also like to see you in person this week, so I can look in your nose and ears and feel that lump properly. That won’t hold up the referral.
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges the examination video cannot provide without delaying referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Work’s the tricky bit. Two appointments…
I understand. This is worth the time, and I can give you a letter for work if it helps. Could you manage early morning for my appointment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the practical barrier rather than overriding it

SCA_MODELS.text: Early is fine. Thanks.

If you have a nosebleed that won’t stop after 15 minutes of pinching, go to A&E. Contact us the same day if you get double vision, numbness in your face, trouble swallowing or breathing, or if the lump grows quickly. And if you haven’t heard about the hospital appointment within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net plus a hand-off check on the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Got it.
So that I know I’ve explained it well, how would you describe today’s plan to someone at home?
Not hay fever. Urgent camera check within two weeks, you’ll see me this week, and I ring if the bleeding’s bad or anything new happens.
Exactly right. You did the right thing coming in. I’ll see you this week.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with a clear summary and follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Wei Chen
pmh: No other significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: E-consult form: several weeks of a blocked right nostril with blood-stained discharge and nosebleeds from the same side. Requests a steroid nasal spray or antihistamines. No previous ENT consultation on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation booked to discuss his nasal symptoms.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG98 (hearing loss in adults, 2018) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Persistent one-sided nasal blockage with blood-stained discharge is not hay fever. With a same-side blocked ear, a neck lump and Southern Chinese family origin, nasopharyngeal carcinoma must be excluded by urgent ENT assessment with nasendoscopy.

points.t: Allergic rhinitis is typically bilateral, with sneezing, itch and clear discharge. Persistent unilateral obstruction, blood-stained discharge or recurrent same-side epistaxis needs examination and ENT assessment: causes range from polyp or septal deviation to sinonasal or nasopharyngeal tumour.

A neck lump (often the first sign), a unilateral middle-ear effusion or blocked ear from Eustachian tube obstruction, nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge, and cranial nerve symptoms such as double vision or facial numbness. Incidence is higher in people of Southern Chinese and south-east Asian family origin; EBV-associated.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with an unexplained lump in the neck, and for oral cancer with a persistent unexplained neck lump. At 52 with an unexplained neck lump he meets this; the head and neck team assesses the nasopharynx too.

NICE NG98 (2018): consider a suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT for adults of Chinese or south-east Asian family origin who have hearing loss and a middle-ear effusion not associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. Confirm the effusion on otoscopy at a face-to-face review.
Video cannot replace anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy and neck palpation. Arrange a prompt face-to-face examination, but the history alone justifies the urgent referral; do not wait for a spray trial.
Heavy epistaxis that will not stop with pressure, or new cranial nerve signs (double vision, facial numbness, drooping), stridor or difficulty swallowing need same-day assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets him describe the one-sided pattern; parks the spray request without dismissing it.
Work pressure and reluctance to take time off; what he has read online; who is at home to support him.
Picks up the withheld neck lump, the “different from my usual hay fever” comment and the same-side blocked ear.
Idea (hay fever or sinus); concern (quiet worry about cancer after reading online); expectation (spray, but also wants certainty).
Face-to-face anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy for effusion and neck examination; nasendoscopy via ENT; no spray trial first.
Nasopharyngeal or sinonasal carcinoma versus polyp, septal deviation, foreign body or infection; allergic rhinitis argued against by the one-sided pattern.
Asks about cranial nerve symptoms, swallowing, weight loss and ethnicity-related risk; recognises the neck lump and unilateral ear as red flags.
States that a tumour must be excluded and explains why this is not hay fever, while acknowledging benign causes.
Suspected cancer pathway referral today (NICE NG12 neck lump criterion; NICE NG98 ear criterion if effusion confirmed); face-to-face examination this week.
Addresses the work barrier practically (early slot, work letter); no allergy treatment as a substitute for referral.
A&E for uncontrolled epistaxis; same-day contact for cranial nerve symptoms, stridor, dysphagia or a fast-growing lump; ring if no appointment within a week.

social.t: Reluctance to take time off is a common reason for delayed presentation. Offer early slots and a letter confirming hospital appointments; urgent appointments should not be traded for work pressure.
Patients who have read about a condition linked to their background may present with a “safe” explanation. Invite the worry explicitly and correct misinformation.

legal.t: Cancer is a disability under the Equality Act from diagnosis. If a diagnosis follows, he is protected from less favourable treatment at work and entitled to reasonable adjustments, including time off for treatment.

professional.t: Family origin changes the prior probability of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is written into NICE NG98. Ask with an explanation and record it; this is good clinical care, not stereotyping.
GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise the limits of a remote consultation. Arrange examination in person, but do not let it delay an urgent referral the history already justifies.
Suspected cancer pathway referrals should be tracked by the practice; tell the patient what to expect and when to chase.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support and the Mouth Cancer Foundation (head and neck) offer information in plain language, including while waiting for tests.

redFlags: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge or recurrent same-side epistaxis
Unexplained neck lump; unilateral blocked ear or middle-ear effusion in an adult
Cranial nerve symptoms (double vision, facial numbness), dysphagia, weight loss; Southern Chinese or south-east Asian family origin
psychosocial: Reluctance to take time off work and to “make a fuss”
What he has read online and how it has affected him
Who is around to support him through urgent tests
ice: Idea: “It’s my hay fever, or a sinus thing.”
Concern: quiet fear about the neck lump and blocked ear after reading online
Expectation: a spray or antihistamine, while wanting to know it’s nothing

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This isn’t behaving like hay fever. One-sided blockage and bleeding for weeks, with the ear blocked on the same side and a lump in the neck, means we need to rule out something growing at the back of the nose, including cancer. Many causes turn out to be harmless, but this needs an urgent specialist look.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Hay fever is like a whole road flooding: both lanes, both sides. When only one lane is blocked, and it keeps bleeding, we look for something sitting in that lane. The specialists have a thin camera that can see right to the back.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been carrying the worry about that lump on your own, and hoping it was hay fever. Let’s get it checked properly and quickly, so you’re not left wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the work pressure and offer an early face-to-face slot and a work letter, so the urgent referral actually happens.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to head and neck ENT today (NICE NG12 neck lump criterion; NICE NG98 if an effusion is confirmed)
Face-to-face examination this week: anterior rhinoscopy, otoscopy, neck
No steroid spray or antihistamine as a substitute for assessment
safetyNet: A&E for a nosebleed that won’t stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Same-day contact for double vision, facial numbness, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or a rapidly growing lump; ring if no appointment within a week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can hold a red-flag rule against a plausible benign story. Candidates fail it by accepting “hay fever”, by missing the questions that reveal the lump and the ear, or by referring without explaining why.

items.fail: Prescribing a steroid nasal spray or antihistamine and asking him to come back if it doesn’t settle.
items.why: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with bleeding needs assessment, not an allergy trial. This is “management not in line with current UK practice” and delays a possible cancer diagnosis.
items.fix: State the one-sided rule and refer: “Hay fever affects both sides; this needs a specialist look.”

items.fail: Never asking about the ear on the same side or about a neck lump.
items.why: He does not volunteer the lump. Without directed questions, the data gathering misses the two features that make the referral urgent.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Any blocked ear on that side? Any lumps in your neck?”

items.fail: Avoiding the question of family origin because it feels awkward.
items.why: Southern Chinese family origin substantially raises the risk of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and appears in NICE NG98. Leaving it out weakens the reasoning.
items.fix: Ask with a reason: “Some conditions are more common in particular communities; can I ask about your background?”

items.fail: Moving straight past the lump he mentions hesitantly and never asking how he feels about it.
items.why: The withheld lump is the cue to his hidden worry. Missing it reads as “does not respond to cues”.
items.fix: “You left the lump off the form. Has it been worrying you more than you’ve said?”

items.fail: Delaying the referral until he can be examined face to face.
items.why: Examination matters, but the history alone justifies urgent referral; waiting risks weeks of delay.
items.fix: Refer today and examine this week in parallel.

items.fail: Saying “it’s probably nothing” or, at the other extreme, “this could be cancer” with no context.
items.why: False reassurance undermines urgency; bare alarm frightens and disengages. Both lose Relating marks.
items.fix: Honest and proportionate: “We need to rule out a cancer; many causes are harmless; finding anything early matters.”

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll be in touch” and no specific safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the triggers (uncontrolled bleeding, double vision, facial numbness, swallowing or breathing problems) and when to chase the appointment.
